claims.text: As-received Q235 carbon steel has a native oxide film composed primarily of Fe3O4.
The integrity of the native Fe3O4 passive layer governs corrosion suppression and onset in Q235 steel.
At room temperature, an intact native oxide layer retards corrosion of Q235 steel in chloride-rich environments.
Elevated temperature thermally activates defect formation in the native oxide film.
Increased oxide-film defect density causes accelerated localized corrosion.
An intact passive film limits electrolyte penetration into the Q235 steel surface.
An intact passive film limits electron transfer and thereby suppresses corrosion.
Film breakdown at elevated temperature promotes pitting through enhanced anodic oxidation.
At approximately 80°C, Q235 steel will have a higher corrosion rate than in a room-temperature chloride environment.
At approximately 80°C, Q235 steel will exhibit more severe localized corrosion than at room temperature.
Artificially enhancing the passive film will reduce corrosion relative to untreated Q235 steel at room temperature.
Artificially enhancing the passive film will reduce corrosion relative to untreated Q235 steel at elevated temperature.
Differences in alloy composition, oxide-film properties, salt identity, or salt concentration may alter the outcomes.
